introduction-why-are-we-paying-for-this.core: Platform teams are cost centres with expensive engineers, so they have to show economic value: time saved, incidents avoided, faster onboarding, cost efficiency. Make the build-vs-buy decision with full costs, and allocate spend fairly.

first_principles.problem: The CFO asks why 10 engineers work on internal tooling, and the answer is 'developers like it'.
derivation: Decide **build vs buy** on total cost.

analogy.title: A company's IT department justifying itself
analogy.story: It has to show how it keeps everyone productive, not just how much it spends.
analogy.breaks: Over-quantifying can miss strategic value, so include qualitative benefits too.

check.q: Why must platform teams demonstrate economic value?
check.a: They're cost centres whose benefits are indirect, so leadership needs evidence of return to keep funding them.

calculating-roi-the-efficiency-dividend.core: Platform ROI = (value gained − platform cost) / platform cost. The main value is the efficiency dividend: developer hours saved × fully loaded hourly cost, measured from before and after data on tasks like deploys, environment setup and debugging.

first_principles.problem: Teams claim 'it saves time' without measuring how much, or what that time is worth.
truths: Developer time has a clear cost.
Time savings scale with the number of users.
derivation: **Subtract** platform cost; express as ROI and payback period.

analogy.title: Installing a faster checkout system
analogy.story: Seconds saved per customer × thousands of customers × staff wage = a clear return.
analogy.breaks: Saved time isn't always redeployed to value, so present it as capacity, not cash.

code.text:
devs, hours_saved_week, rate = 300, 3, 100
value = devs * hours_saved_week * 46 * rate   # ≈ $4.1M/yr
cost = 8 * 250_000                              # platform team ≈ $2M/yr
print((value - cost) / cost)                    # ≈ 1.07 → 107% ROI

check.a: The value of developer time saved: hours saved × number of developers × fully loaded hourly cost.

indirect-value-stability-and-onboarding.core: Beyond time saved, platforms create indirect value: fewer and shorter incidents (revenue and reputation protected), faster onboarding (new hires productive in days instead of weeks), better security and compliance (reduced breach and audit risk), and talent retention.

first_principles.problem: Measuring only time saved undersells platforms that mostly prevent costly problems.
derivation: **Incidents**: fewer × cost per incident (revenue, engineering hours).
**Retention**: improved developer satisfaction reduces costly attrition.

analogy.title: A building's fire suppression system
analogy.story: Its value isn't time saved but disasters prevented and insurance premiums reduced.
analogy.breaks: Counterfactuals (incidents that didn't happen) are estimates, so be transparent about the assumptions.

example.title: Quantifying indirect value
example.outcome: the full picture of platform value.

check.q: Give two sources of indirect platform value.
check.a: For example, fewer incidents (avoided revenue loss) and faster onboarding of new engineers.

build-vs-buy-the-eternal-struggle.core: Build when a capability differentiates you or no product fits. Buy (or adopt open source) when it's a commodity. Compare total cost of ownership over 3–5 years (licences vs engineers, maintenance, opportunity cost), plus time-to-value and strategic fit.

first_principles.problem: Teams build internal portals, secrets managers and CI systems that commercial or open-source tools already do well.
truths: Buying costs licences and some flexibility.
derivation: Ask: is it a **differentiator**? (Wardley: genesis or custom → build).
Compute **TCO**: build (team × years + ops) vs buy (licences + integration).
Consider **OSS + support** as a middle path.

analogy.title: Baking your own bread vs. buying it
analogy.story: A bakery's signature loaf is worth making in-house; a restaurant's side bread is better bought.
analogy.breaks: Buying creates vendor dependency, so check exit options.

example.title: Portal decision
flow: Build custom portal: 4 engineers × 3 yrs ≈ $3M + upkeep

check.q: When is building internally usually justified?
check.a: When the capability differentiates your business or no available product fits your needs.

the-hidden-costs-of-building-the-iceberg.core: 'I can build that in a weekend' sees only the tip of the iceberg. The hidden costs are maintenance, security patches, upgrades, scaling, on-call, documentation, user support, onboarding and the opportunity cost of not building something else, often 5–10x the initial build.

first_principles.problem: A homegrown tool built in a sprint becomes a permanent burden owned by whoever's left.
truths: Engineers working on tools aren't working on products.
derivation: List **lifecycle costs**: maintenance, security, upgrades, scaling, support.

analogy.title: Owning a boat
analogy.story: The purchase price is small next to mooring, maintenance, insurance and repairs.
analogy.breaks: Bought tools have hidden costs too (integration, vendor management), so compare like with like.

example.title: A homegrown feature flag service
flow: Year 1: SDKs for 4 languages, HA, audit log

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: A SaaS licence would have cost less.

example.outcome: build decisions that count the whole iceberg.

check.q: Why is 'I can build it in a weekend' misleading?
check.a: It ignores the ongoing maintenance, security, scaling, support and opportunity costs, which far exceed the initial build.

chargeback-vs-showback-who-pays.core: A central cloud bill hides who consumes what. Showback reports costs to teams for awareness, while chargeback actually bills teams' budgets for accountability. Platform services need fair allocation of shared costs either way.

first_principles.problem: A $500k/month bill sits on the VP's card, and teams have no idea, or incentive, to use resources efficiently.
derivation: Move to **chargeback** when the data is trusted.
Avoid **perverse incentives** (teams bypassing the platform to save cost).

analogy.title: Splitting a household electricity bill
analogy.story: Showing each flatmate their usage builds awareness; making them pay their share builds accountability.
analogy.breaks: Aggressive chargeback can discourage using the shared platform, so price it thoughtfully.

example.title: Rolling out showback
flow: Tag and allocate cloud + platform costs

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Teams start optimising their own usage.

check.q: What's a risk of aggressive chargeback for platform services?
check.a: Teams may bypass the shared platform to avoid charges, recreating duplication and shadow IT.

pricing-models-for-internal-platform-ser.core: Under chargeback, platform services need internal prices: cost-plus (cloud cost + platform overhead), usage-based (per vCPU-hour, per GB), tiered bundles (small/medium/large environments) or subsidised (free to encourage adoption). Prices should be simple, predictable and encourage the desired behaviour.

first_principles.problem: Passing raw, complex AWS line items to teams is confusing and unpredictable.
derivation: **Subsidised**: zero or low price for strategic adoption.

analogy.title: A company cafeteria's pricing
analogy.story: Simple set meals (tiers), à la carte (usage) or free coffee to encourage people to stay on site (subsidy).
analogy.breaks: Over-engineered internal billing costs more than it's worth.

example.title: A tiered environment price list
flow: Small env (2 vCPU, 4 GB, small DB): $300/mo

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Predictable bills, and the right behaviour encouraged.

check.q: Why might a platform subsidise some services internally?
check.a: To encourage adoption of strategic capabilities (golden paths) instead of costly custom setups.
